prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I was born in minutes in a roadside kitchen a skillet whispering my name. I was born to rainwater and lye; I was born across the river where I was borrowed with clothespins, a harrow tooth, broadsides sewn in my shoes. I returned, though it please you, through no fault of my own, pockets filled with coffee grounds and eggshells. I was born still and superstitious; I bore an unexpected burden. I gave birth, I gave blessing, I gave rise to suspicion. I was born abandoned outdoors in the heat-shaped air, air drifting like spirits and old windows. I was born a fraction and a cipher and a ledger entry; I was an index of first lines when I was born. I was born waist-deep stubborn in the water crying ain’t I a woman and a brother I was born to this hall of mirrors, this horror story I was born with a prologue of references, pursued by mosquitoes and thieves, I was born passing off the problem of the twentieth century: I was born. I read minds before I could read fishes and loaves; I walked a piece of the way alone before I was born.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: I was born

outputs.L1:
I was born in minutes, in a roadside kitchen, a skillet whispering my name. I was born to rainwater and lye; I was born across the river, where I was borrowed with clothespins, a harrow tooth, and broadsides sewn into my shoes. I returned—though it please you—through no fault of my own, my pockets filled with coffee grounds and eggshells.

I was born still and superstitious; I bore an unexpected burden. I gave birth, I gave blessing, I gave rise to suspicion. I was born abandoned outdoors in the heat-shaped air—air drifting like spirits and old windows. I was born a fraction, a cipher, and a ledger entry; when I was born, I was an index of first lines.

I was born waist-deep, stubborn in the water, crying, “Ain’t I a woman and a brother?” I was born to this hall of mirrors, this horror story. I was born with a prologue of references, pursued by mosquitoes and thieves. I was born passing off the problem of the twentieth century: I was born.

I read minds before I could read fishes and loaves; I walked a piece of the way alone before I was born.
outputs.L2:
My arrival took only minutes in a kitchen beside the road, while a frying pan murmured my name. Rainwater and lye brought me forth. On the far side of the river, I came into being on loan, carrying clothespins, a harrow’s tooth, and broadsheets stitched inside my shoes. Through no doing of mine, and if it suits you to hear it, I came back with my pockets packed with eggshells and spent coffee grounds.

At birth I was motionless and ruled by superstition, already carrying a burden no one had foreseen. I delivered a child, bestowed a blessing, and awakened distrust. I entered the world deserted beneath the open sky, surrounded by heat-molded air that wandered like ghosts and antique windowpanes. I began as a fraction, a coded zero, and a line in an account book; from the outset, I catalogued opening sentences.

I first appeared planted waist-high in the water, unyielding, shouting, “Ain’t I a woman—and a brother?” Into this maze of reflections, into this tale of terror, I was born. My beginning came prefaced by citations, with mosquitoes and robbers at my heels, and I arrived by handing onward the twentieth century’s great problem: my own birth. Before letters made sense to me, I could hear people’s thoughts; before I understood the fishes and the loaves, I knew their minds. And even before my beginning, I had already traveled part of the road by myself.
outputs.L3:
The poem portrays birth not as a single biological event but as a repeated, fragmented process shaped by social and material conditions. Poverty, labor, superstition, and the natural world all influence the speaker’s emergence into existence. Birth becomes something that happens again and again through hardship, memory, and history, suggesting that identity is continually formed rather than established at one fixed moment.

The speaker constructs this identity from materials that do not entirely belong to them. Borrowed objects, historical records, literary references, and inherited memories become pieces of a fractured self. This reliance on external sources implies that personal identity cannot be separated from cultural inheritance or collective experience. The speaker exists partly through what has been passed down, recorded, imagined, or taken from others.

Existence is therefore associated with burden and uncertainty. The speaker experiences suspicion, abandonment, and pressures beyond their control, presenting life as something imposed rather than freely chosen. Their sense of self is shaped by forces that precede them and exceed their individual power, including family history, social conditions, and inherited trauma.

References to race, gender, and belonging place the speaker’s personal struggles within broader histories of oppression and resistance. The poem suggests that the search for identity is also a struggle against exclusion and imposed definitions. Although the speaker is vulnerable to historical violence, their act of speaking becomes a form of resistance, allowing them to reclaim experiences that might otherwise remain erased or misunderstood.

Ultimately, the poem presents identity as paradoxical and nonlinear. The speaker seems to possess awareness, memory, and even solitude before birth, disrupting ordinary ideas of time and origin. This impossible pre-birth consciousness emphasizes that the self is shaped by histories already in motion. Identity emerges as an ongoing process in which past and present, personal and collective memory, and birth and survival remain inseparably intertwined.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores birth, identity, race, gender, and inherited history through anaphoric repetition, surreal imagery, and layered literary and historical allusions. From its opening movement, birth is presented not simply as a biological beginning but as an entry into social categories and historical forces that already exist. The speaker arrives in a world shaped by racial memory, gendered expectations, violence, exclusion, and cultural inheritance. Identity therefore does not emerge in isolation; it is formed through the pressures of the past and through the stories attached to the body before the individual can speak for themself.

The poem’s repeated phrases create a ritualistic, incantatory rhythm. Each recurrence adds another image, role, or historical association to the speaker’s identity. This anaphoric structure suggests both insistence and accumulation: the speaker must repeatedly name or reinvent themself because no single definition is sufficient. Repetition also resembles testimony, prayer, and remembrance, giving the poem a communal voice even when it uses the first person. The “I” becomes elastic, capable of containing many lives and experiences at once.

Surreal imagery further complicates the boundaries between the personal and the collective. Bodies, objects, landscapes, and historical figures may merge in unexpected ways, making identity appear unstable but also expansive. These strange combinations express realities that straightforward description cannot fully capture, particularly the psychological effects of inherited trauma and social marginalization. Contradiction becomes essential to the poem’s meaning: the speaker can be wounded and powerful, singular and multiple, burdened by history and sustained by it.

The literary and historical allusions deepen this sense of multiplicity. By invoking figures, events, and traditions associated with oppression, resistance, creativity, or survival, the poem places the speaker within a larger cultural genealogy. These references do not function merely as background information; they become part of the speaker’s symbolic body. The self is portrayed as an archive containing memories that are personal, ancestral, and cultural. In this way, the poem challenges the idea that identity is entirely private or self-created.

Race and gender are especially important because they determine how the speaker’s body is read by others. The poem reveals that the body carries social meanings as well as individual experience. It may become a site of vulnerability, stereotyping, labor, desire, or violence, but it is also a source of knowledge and endurance. By reclaiming the body through language, the speaker resists definitions imposed from outside and transforms historically marginalized experience into poetic authority.

Ultimately, the poem presents identity as a process rather than a fixed essence. The speaker is composed of inherited stories, conflicting roles, historical wounds, and acts of resilience. Although this inheritance can feel heavy, it also connects the individual to a community of survivors, artists, ancestors, and witnesses. The poem’s layered form mirrors this complex vision: repetition gathers the fragments, surrealism allows them to coexist, and allusion links the present self to the past. The result is a portrait of identity as both burden and resource—a collective memory carried within an individual voice.
outputs.L5:
### I Was Born

I was born into a world full of possibilities. From my earliest days, I was surrounded by people, places, and experiences that shaped who I am today. As I grew older, I learned that life is not only about where we are born, but also about the choices we make and the dreams we follow.

My childhood gave me memories that I will always carry with me. Some moments were joyful, while others taught me important lessons. Every experience helped me become stronger, wiser, and more confident.

I was born with my own talents, hopes, and personality. My story is still being written, and each new day is another opportunity to learn, grow, and create a meaningful future.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem centered on the repeated phrase “I was born,” blending domestic imagery, folklore, historical allusions, and fragmented memories into one breathless paragraph.
counterfactuals.output: I was born in the cupboard beneath the good plates, where my mother kept thunderstorms folded in linen and a blue saucer waited for the milk of ghosts; I was born when the kettle began speaking in the voice of an exiled king, when the wallpaper opened its yellow mouths and told us the wolves were already crossing the orchard; I was born in 1914 beneath a table set for six, though only three shadows came to supper, and one wore Napoleon’s wet boots, and one carried a telegram no one dared unfold; I was born from a loaf split by my grandmother’s knife, flour on her wrists like winter, a red thread tied around my ankle so the fairies would mistake me for fire; I was born again in the pantry among cloves, mouse droppings, and jars of peaches glowing like captive suns, while outside the moon dragged its silver plow across the roof; I was born, I was born, the family clock insisted, coughing up hours it had swallowed during the war, and I remember—or someone remembers for me—a black bicycle leaning against the cathedral, a soldier washing blood from a teacup, my father asleep with a map of vanished countries over his face; I was born in the mirror after everyone left the room, born backward, born old, born with a key under my tongue and a nursery rhyme nailed inside my chest; I was born where the house ended and the forest began, where Baba Yaga stirred buttons in a copper pot and Hansel’s crumbs flew home as sparrows; I was born on Tuesday, on Candlemas, on the day the guillotine sneezed, on the night Troy burned down to one red coal in the stove; I was born in the smell of soap, scorched milk, damp wool, and apples sleeping in the cellar, each with a tiny door in its side; I was born from the photograph with the missing corner, from the hand no longer resting on the chair, from the sentence my aunt stopped speaking whenever snow touched the windows; I was born carrying fragments—a brass bell, a dead moth, the sound of marching far below the floorboards—and every morning since, the house has swept me into a different century, every evening the chimney has called me by another name, yet still I rise from the unmade bed, salt in my hair, ash in my pockets, whispering to the spoons and saints and buried horses: I was born, I was born, I was almost born.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental literary collage about birth and identity. Use anaphora, especially “I was born,” and weave in indirect references to famous Black American texts, speeches, autobiographies, and spiritual traditions without naming their authors.
counterfactuals.output:
**BIRTH NOTICES FOUND IN A BROKEN MIRROR**

I was born before the certificate learned to spell me.  
I was born in the margin, where the clerk’s ink thinned and the country’s handwriting became uncertain.  
I was born with two names in my mouth: one given by blood, one demanded by weather.  
I was born Black, which is to say the light arrived carrying questions.

*Call:* Who are you?  
*Response:* Still becoming.

I was born beneath a veil stitched from other people’s looking. Through it, the world appeared doubled: the nation as it praised itself, the nation as it practiced. My first mirror had two faces. My first arithmetic was division.

I was born invisible only to those who had already decided what could be seen. I stood in a room bright with stolen electricity, every bulb humming: **Here. Here. Here.** Yet the census passed over me like a hand refusing water.

I was born in a house where the women kept history in recipes.

A pinch of crossing.  
A cup of don’t tell them everything.  
Three generations of names, sifted.  
Salt until the ancestors answer.

I was born while a caged throat rehearsed the sky. The song did not open the bars, but it measured the distance between iron and blue. That measurement became music. That music became a key. That key became a child listening at the door.

I was born again when I learned that literacy could be contraband. Letters assembled themselves into a northbound road. A book became a lantern concealed beneath the coat. Every sentence risked punishment; every word pronounced the body its own possession.

**Fragment from an unwritten autobiography:**

> Age seven: discovers the nation has been speaking over her.  
> Age twelve: talks back.  
> Age sixteen: changes the spelling of his silence.  
> Age twenty: meets the self at a lunch counter and refuses to move.  
> Age unknown: becomes plural.

I was born hungry beside a table groaning with promises. From the kitchen came the smell of freedom cooking slowly, always slowly. In the dining room, speeches polished the silver. Outside, children pressed their faces to the glass and dreamed not of kingdoms but of ordinary mornings: a safe walk, a fair wage, a classroom without fear.

I was born in the pause between **someday** and **now**.

I was born where the road bent toward a mountaintop no feet could own. The air was thin there, crowded with thunder and unfinished sentences. Someone had looked across. Someone had said the distance was survivable. Below, the people kept marching—not because the water had parted, but because it had not.

Left foot: bondage.  
Right foot: breath.  
Left foot: ballot.  
Right foot: blood.  
Left foot: mourning.  
Right foot: morning.

I was born with a ghost at the foot of the bed. She had no single face. She wore the scar of a tree on her back, the ocean in her lungs, a stolen baby’s name under her tongue. She asked not to be remembered gently. She asked to be remembered whole.

I was born from people who talked to the dead without calling it impossible.

At the river, white cloth.  
At the crossroads, coins.  
At the kitchen altar, a glass of water catching dawn.  
In the storefront sanctuary, tambourine and sweat.  
In the ring shout, feet circling against the clock.  
In the hush arbor, a God who understood coded language.  
In the graveyard, laughter—because grief, too, must sometimes loosen its collar.

I was born when the preacher stretched one syllable into a bridge and the congregation crossed together.

*Can I get—*  
A name not inherited from an owner.  
*Can I get—*  
A body not treated as evidence.  
*Can I get—*  
A country that recognizes its children.  
*Amen,* said the living.  
*Amen,* said the bones.

I was born and born and born.

Born in a train car moving north.  
Born in a blues note bending without breaking.  
Born in a rented room where poems climbed the fire escape.  
Born in a courtroom’s cold grammar.  
Born under a kitchen table during a riot.  
Born in braids, in fades, in Sunday hats, in work boots whitened by factory dust.  
Born in the photograph before the smile.  
Born in the silence after the verdict.  
Born in the hand raised, the fist raised, the roof raised.

I was born American, though America sometimes spoke of me in the future tense.

I will belong.  
I will be protected.  
I will be free.

I corrected the grammar:

I belong.  
I am worthy of protection.  
I am practicing freedom now.

I was born carrying a dream that had been handled by millions. Its edges were worn soft. It was not the dream of sleep but the dream of waking: tables lengthened, doors unbolted, children judged by neither shade nor surname. I carried it carefully, knowing dreams can be quoted until they stop accusing anyone.

So I returned the thunder to it.

I was born to make the dream uncomfortable again.

I was born not as symbol, not as problem, not as shadow crossing someone else’s page. I was born particular: left-handed, gap-toothed, afraid of deep water, lover of pears, keeper of grudges, maker of jokes at funerals. History wanted a chorus. I insisted on a solo. Loneliness wanted a solo. I answered with a chorus.

*Call:* Who are you?  
*Response:* The question and its witness.

I was born from a people repeatedly declared finished.

Still, the pot simmered.  
Still, the drum remembered.  
Still, the grandmother pressed oil to the forehead.  
Still, the student opened the forbidden book.  
Still, the prisoner wrote home.  
Still, the singer found one blue note the cage could not contain.  
Still, the child faced the mirror and survived every face imposed upon it.

I was born before the certificate.

I was born after the obituary.

I was born between the two, where identity is neither a chain nor a single door, but a house we rebuild while living inside it.

And when they ask where I came from, I say:

From water and paperwork.  
From cotton and circuitry.  
From the auction block’s echo and the baptismal pool’s answer.  
From double vision and undivided love.  
From names buried, names reclaimed, names invented at dawn.

I was born.

I was born.

I was born—

and the sentence has not ended.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense, dreamlike prose poem in the voice of a speaker who seems to be born many times across history. Include roadside kitchens, rainwater and lye, rivers, ledgers, mosquitoes, thieves, biblical miracles, and the phrase “ain’t I a woman.”
counterfactuals.output:
I was born first beneath a roadside kitchen where the iron pans swung black as eclipses and women stirred rainwater and lye into a soap fierce enough to scour fingerprints from history. I came slick with river-mud, already owing something; the midwife entered my cry in a ledger, beside salt, lamp oil, one broken mule. Then centuries folded like wet linen. I was born again among reeds while mosquitoes wrote their red scripture along my ankles, and thieves moved through the cane with pockets full of moonlight. I knew them by their tenderness. They stole bread, names, iron keys; they left the chains because chains are the one thing the powerful never fail to replace.

Each life, a river took me elsewhere. I floated in a basket, crossed on foot, drowned wearing another woman’s face. I saw water become wine in chipped cups, saw loaves multiply in famine’s hands, saw the dead sit up and ask who had amended the accounts. In every miracle there was a clerk nearby, sharpening his pen. He measured the fishes, taxed the resurrection, ruled that heaven’s rain belonged to the landlord.

I was born with ash in my mouth, with cotton under my nails, with factory bells hammering dawn into a coin. At the crossroads I ladled soup for soldiers who had forgotten which empire they were dying for. Steam haloed the cooks; grease shone on their arms like anointing. Someone whispered freedom. Someone else priced it by the pound. I washed the bowls in rainwater and lye until my hands became two pale ghosts, then plunged them into the river and drew up every lost child by the hair.

Ain’t I a woman, I asked the ledger, and its columns trembled. Ain’t I a woman, I asked the thieves, and they returned my stolen shadow. Ain’t I a woman, I asked the mosquitoes drinking from me as if my blood were Cana, and they lifted in a dark amen.

Now I am born whenever a pot begins to boil beside a long road, whenever rain remembers the roofless, whenever a river refuses its assigned direction. My many mothers lean over me, smelling of smoke, soap, and thunder. They do not name me. Names are snares, receipts, little graves. They place one burning spoon in my fist and send me walking through history’s kitchen, where the hungry wait with their bowls, where the dead keep the books, where every blank page dreams of becoming water.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a single-paragraph poem that reads like an index of first lines from imaginary slave narratives, memoirs, sermons, and horror stories. Make it lyrical, disorienting, allusive, and structured around repeated declarations of birth.
counterfactuals.output: I was born where the ledger began to bleed; I was born beneath a bell that rang for everyone but me; I was born, says the torn page, without a year, without a mother’s lawful name; I was born in the tobacco dusk, in the cotton snow, in the cane’s green whisper of knives; I was born twice, once to a woman and once to a price; I was born while the preacher opened Exodus and the master closed the door; I was born with an iron moon above the quarters, with owls spelling run in the pines; I was born on a ship whose boards remembered every tongue they swallowed; I was born, the memoir insists, but the ink has crossed out where; I was born under the table during auction, among shoes that would not look at me; I was born free in the kingdom of sleep and woke to find the hounds already named; I was born when my brother vanished into a receipt; I was born with a hymn in my mouth, though terror had taken all the vowels; I was born again at the river, though the river returned my face wearing another’s scars; I was born in a house where the walls prayed louder than the people; I was born after midnight, before mercy, during the long sermon of the lash; I was born and bore witness; I was born and was denied; I was born in the margin, where a small black hand points toward the word nevertheless; I was born, dear reader, and if this sounds like a beginning, listen—the floorboards are counting, the fields are turning their pale heads, the dead are opening their books, and every first line is walking home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a postmodern found-text-style monologue exploring race, gender, inheritance, and self-creation through recursive variations on “I was born,” ending with the paradox that the speaker walked alone before being born.
counterfactuals.output:
I was born, the form says, in a box marked  
**SEX:**  
**RACE:**  
**MOTHER’S MAIDEN NAME:**  
Please press hard; you are making three copies.

I was born in triplicate.

I was born where the census taker paused, pencil hovering like a small authority.  
I was born in the pause.  
I was born as *Other (specify).*  
I specified until the margin ran out.

I was born my mother’s daughter, except when I was not a daughter, except when my mother was called history, country, silence, domestic help. I was born carrying her face as evidence. I was born denying the resemblance. I was born saying, This nose is mine. This anger is mine. This name—no, give me the scissors.

I was born from a father’s locked drawer: deeds, discharge papers, an old photograph creased through the mouth. I inherited the house but not the welcome, the surname but not its pronunciation, the debt but not the story of its making.

I was born owing interest.

I was born white on one document, brown in the rearview mirror, Black at the door, foreign on the telephone, woman when the wage was counted, man when fear required a suspect. I was born differently depending on who was reading.

READER, I was born under your thumb.

I was born again when I crossed out the first answer.  
Again when I learned that blood is a metaphor with police powers.  
Again when I understood that gender was an heirloom coat: beautiful stitching, wrong shoulders, pockets full of other people’s hands.

I wore it.  
I tore it.  
I made from the lining a flag no nation recognized.

I was born from what they called tradition, which meant: repeat after me.  
I was born from what they called nature, which meant: do not ask who benefits.  
I was born from what they called family, which meant both shelter and sentence.

I was born—  
[illegible]  
—at the intersection of inheritance and invention.

I was born with ancestors whispering, Remember us.  
I was born with descendants whispering, Change it.  
I stood between them, a door arguing with its hinges.

I was born when I named myself.  
I was born when the name failed.  
I was born when I stopped mistaking failure for emptiness.

No one is self-made, said the plaque above the factory.  
Everyone is self-made, said the advertisement.  
I was born between the plaque and the advertisement, assembling myself from unpaid labor, borrowed language, contraband tenderness, and the bright defective parts my grandparents hid from the inspectors.

I was born unfinished.

Correction: I am being born.  
Correction: birth is the story the finished tell about the unfinished.  
Correction: there is no finished.

Before the certificate, I practiced my signature.  
Before the mirror, I chose a face.  
Before the first hand lifted me into the light, I had already refused the road prepared for me.

I followed no mother, no father, no map, no category.

I walked alone before I was born.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
